# Ummādantījātaka (Ja 527)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Ummādantījātaka* (Ja 527) is a canonical birth story in the Jātaka collection of the Pali Tipiṭaka [SuttaCentral]. The framing story opens at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī, where the Buddha delivers the discourse on the occasion of a monk who has become infatuated and distressed after catching sight of an exquisitely adorned woman while walking on his alms round [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1891].
Characterized in modern scholarship as a dramatic ballad or dramatic legend [Nariman 1919; Mylius 2003], the past narrative focuses on Ummadantī, daughter of the merchant Tirītavaccha in Ariṭṭhapura [Martin 2006; Fausböll 1897]. Her epithet evokes intoxicating, captivating beauty, which in Buddhist narrative lore was acquired as the result of a past-life deed of giving: having painstakingly woven a robe over two years to offer to an ascetic, she accompanied the gift with an earnest aspiration (*patthanā*) for beauty [Fenn 1994; Khosla 1989]. In the story, the Bodhisatta is reborn as the king of the Sivis, whose general and close friend is Ahipāraka, the husband of Ummadantī [Martin 2006; Mylius 2003; Fausböll 1891]. The king catches sight of Ummadantī and becomes desperately infatuated, falling sick with forbidden desire [Martin 2006; Mylius 2003]. When Ahipāraka discovers the cause of the king's torment, he nobly offers to surrender his wife to his master, but through righteous reflection and the general’s moral instruction, the king masters his lust and restores his composure [Mylius 2003; Fausböll 1891]. At the close of the story, the king is revealed to be the Bodhisatta, Ahipāraka is identified with Sāriputta, the charioteer Sunanda with Ānanda, and Ummadantī with Uppalavaṇṇā [Fausböll 1891].
SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus agree on substantive text reuse between the *Ummādantījātaka* and other Pali works, notably in shared righteous-rule verses (§§47–51) that also occur in the *Adhammikasutta* (AN 4.70), the *Rājovādajātaka* (Ja 334), the *Mahābodhijātaka* (Ja 528), and the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna* chapter of the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. These gnomic verses are likewise cited across later exegetical and anthology literature, including the *Nettivibhāvinī*, the *Kavidappaṇanīti*, and the *Sāsanavaṃsappadīpikā* [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language matches identified by DharmaNexus show shared lines and narrative parallels with the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna* and Tibetan translations of works including the *Vinayavastu*, the *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottamasūtra* [DharmaNexus].
